chunks: What happens in a load transient. The question: Explain what happens during a load transient event.
A load transient is a sudden change in the current the load draws. The inductor current cannot jump, because an inductor resists fast changes.
So at first the output capacitor supplies the missing current and the output voltage dips.
The control loop then raises the duty cycle, the inductor current climbs, and the output recovers.
Picture a bucket under a slow tap. Water flows out at a steady rate and the tap refills it just as fast. Suddenly you open the drain wider.
The bucket level drops, because the tap takes a moment to open up and match. Only when the tap is flowing as much as the drain does the level stop falling.
The bucket is the capacitor and the tap is the inductor. The analogy leaves out ESR, which adds an instant step.
The order matters. The minimum voltage is at stage G, not when the duty cycle first moves. The shape after G is set by the loop.
Load transient (step): a sudden jump in load current. Droop: how far the output voltage dips during a step-up.
Slew rate: how fast the inductor current can rise, (V in-V out) over L ("What sets the inductor current slope").
ESR: the small resistance in the capacitor, which adds an instant I times ESR step. Loop delay: the time the feedback loop takes to react.
A 12 volts to 3. 3 volts buck has a 4. 7 microhenries inductor and a 47 microfarads capacitor. The load steps from 1 amps to 3 amps. The inductor can only rise at 8. 7 over 4.
7 micro about 1. 85 amps/µs, so it needs about 1. 1 microseconds to reach 3 amps. Meanwhile the capacitor covers the 2 amps gap and falls at 2 over 47 micro about 0.
043 volts per microsecond at first. That is the whole idea.
"When the load steps up, the inductor current can't jump, since it only ramps at V in minus V out over L, so the output capacitor supplies the extra current.
You see an immediate ESR step, then the capacitor droops at delta I over C.
The loop senses the droop, raises the duty cycle, and the inductor ramps up until its current matches the new load, at which point the droop bottoms out.
The inductor then overshoots slightly to recharge the capacitor and the output settles, ringing according to the phase margin.
A load release is the mirror image, and it overshoots more because the inductor only falls at V out over L."
Quick check. When does the output voltage reach its minimum after a load step-up (ignoring ESR)?
